overview: A boost converter does the opposite job of a buck converter: it takes a lower input voltage and produces a higher output voltage — useful for running 5V electronics from a single 3.7V LiPo cell, or generating a higher voltage for a specific component from a lower battery voltage. It sounds like it's creating energy from nothing, but it isn't — output current drops as voltage rises, since power in roughly equals power out (minus conversion losses); a boost converter that doubles voltage will supply roughly half the current a linear supply at the same input could, which is a common point of confusion for beginners expecting both higher voltage and unchanged current for free.
simpleSummary: A small circuit that turns a lower battery voltage into a higher one.

specifications.outputVoltage: Adjustable, commonly up to 28V depending on module
specifications.outputCurrent: Decreases as the voltage step-up ratio increases (power conservation)

pinMap.name: IN+
pinMap.function: Positive voltage input, often from a single-cell battery.
pinMap.currentLimit: Depends on required output current and step-up ratio

pinMap.name: OUT+
pinMap.function: Regulated (higher) positive output, adjustable via onboard trimpot.
pinMap.currentLimit: Decreases as output voltage increases relative to input
pinMap.gotcha: Don't expect the same current at 12V out that you'd get running the load directly at the battery's native 3.7V — available current drops roughly in proportion to the voltage step-up.

useCases.title: Single-cell to 5V USB power
useCases.scenario: Run 5V electronics or charge a USB device from a single 3.7V LiPo cell.

useCases.title: High-voltage component supply from low-voltage battery
useCases.scenario: Generate a higher voltage needed by a specific component (e.g. some sensor or display types) from a lower main battery voltage.

oftenConfusedWith: LM2596 buck converter (steps voltage down, not up)
oftenUpgradedTo: Buck-boost converters that handle both step-up and step-down automatically as input voltage varies
